query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing an on‐the‐fly active learning strategy to dynamically refine machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLPs) during phase-transition simulations will significantly reduce the computational cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties while retaining near-DFT fidelity.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental or binary systems at temperatures near their fusion point, with well-characterized ab initio free energy landscapes for both solid and fluid states.
generation.intervention: Replace full-scale ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) with an active-learning assisted MLP framework that selectively triggers ab initio (DFT) calculations in regions of high uncertainty during simulation of the phase transition.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted near melting temperatures where vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling are critical; most applicable for elemental and binary systems and potentially extendable to multicomponent systems with further validation.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLP’s adaptive capability to update its parameters based on local atomic configurations during high-uncertainty events mediates the balance between simulation cost and the accuracy of free energy and entropy estimates.
generation.mechanism: By actively learning only in critical regions of the configuration space where the potential’s prediction error is high, the method minimizes unnecessary ab initio evaluations; this yields accurate free-energy surfaces and entropy contributions while substantially reducing overall computational demand.
generation.predicted_outcome: A marked reduction in computational cost (targeting an order-of-magnitude improvement over AIMD and TOR-TILD) with free energy predictions and derived thermodynamic observables (e.g., melting point, latent heat) within acceptable error margins relative to full AIMD simulations.
generation.baseline: Standard explicit ab initio molecular dynamics simulations and TOR-TILD workflows that compute free energies continuously without adaptive updates.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to perform best for systems with relatively moderate configurational complexity (elemental or binary) near the fusion temperature; its extension to multicomponent high-entropy systems may encounter additional challenges due to more complex phase spaces.
generation.uncertainty: The exact cost savings and accuracy retention in systems with extreme anharmonicity or complex electronic interactions remain uncertain, necessitating further benchmarking especially in multicomponent materials.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the active-learning MLP framework to simulate the solid-to-liquid phase transition in a well-characterized elemental or binary system. Compare the fusion free energy curves, melting temperatures, and vibrational entropy estimates against those obtained from full AIMD simulations. Monitor the frequency and impact of adaptive ab initio updates triggered by high uncertainty.
measurements: Fusion free energy curves for both solid and fluid phases
Vibrational entropy and other thermodynamic contributions
Total computational cost (CPU/GPU hours) and number of triggered ab initio calculations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the active-learning MLP framework fails to reproduce AIMD-calculated free energies and related thermodynamic observables within an acceptable error margin (e.g., deviations >5%) or if it does not achieve at least an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared to full AIMD/TOR-TILD workflows.

cited_evidence.text: Another alternative to traditional supercell methods are machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) that are trained on ab initio data. The size of supercells is not limited with MLIPs, which is especially important when simulating extended defects like interfaces, where proper configurational averaging becomes an issue with MPEAs. In contrast to the previously proposed way of passively training general-purpose interatomic potentials on a pre-defined fixed training set (e.g.,,,), whose accuracy is not sufficient for our goals, especially for parts of the configurational space not covered by the training set, the use of active learning enables automatic generation of MLIP training sets specifically tailored to a given class of systems and a given set of properties. This allows one to predict any material property of interest with DFT accuracy over the entire composition space of an alloy, with a minimal amount of DFT calculations. In this work, we combine the two approaches—CPA and actively learned Moment Tensor Potentials (MTP), a class of MLIPs—to characterize solid solution strengthening and ductility of refractory MPEAs. An empirical potential for non-magnetic NiCoCr has been developed in the formalism of EAM, by matching a large ab initio database established for the ternary system without explicit consideration of spin polarization. The ab initio database includes a large set of atomic configurations with corresponding cohesive energies, atomic forces, and stress tensors. A similar force-matching method has previously been employed to develop a highly optimized potential for the Zr-Cu-Al system. In this work, special attention has been paid to the energetics of the stacking faults and chemical ordering of Ni–Co–Cr SSs. In order to give an accurate account of the Ni–Co–Cr system in the full compositional range, more than 3000 atomic configurations were selected to build a comprehensive ab initio database from non-spin-polarized DFT calculations. The atomic configurations not only encompass all the intermetallic compounds reported in the Ni–Co–Cr system but also include liquid/glass structures, various types of defects, transition pathways, and so on, covered in a large pressure–temperature phase space of Ni–Co–Cr.
